move: Lays down the proportionality rule that a cause known only through its effect may be credited with no qualities beyond those requisite to produce it, using Zeuxis's picture to block any inference to further designs or performances.
Treats creation as applying only to beings as noumena, arguing this leaves freedom in the sensible world untouched, without arguing from design to a creator at all.

Concedes that the beauty and fitness of final causes strike with irresistible force where intelligence and design are concerned, while denying that any view of human life supports inferring the moral attributes.

Attacks the analogy between the universe and houses or machines, denying that a conclusion can be transferred from a part to the whole and asking what privileges 'this little agitation of the brain which we call thought' as the model of the universe.
Turns the analogy against itself by arguing the world resembles an animal or vegetable more than a watch, so its cause is more probably something like generation or vegetation than contrivance.

Grants that order, design, and greatness license inferring a wise, good, powerful Author, but denies this reaches all-perfection and downgrades the extension to a permitted conclusion rather than a strict inference, leaving the conception of God inadequately determined.

Argues that stripped of experience every conceivable system of the world is equally possible, and that even on opening his eyes a man could not assign the cause of a single event, much less of the whole universe, since experience alone reveals causes.

Notes that the anti-Epicureans treat the universe as a singular unparalleled effect proving an equally singular cause, allows their reasoning merits attention, and flags the difficulty of reasoning back from cause to effect.

Accepts that the sole argument for a deity runs from the order of nature back to a cause, then applies the ten-ounce-weight analogy to insist no qualities beyond those exactly sufficient may be ascribed, making anything further mere licence of conjecture.
Argues only that adequate ideas in the human mind follow from God insofar as he constitutes that mind's essence, saying nothing about inferring a creator from the world's design.

Reduces natural theology to the single undefined proposition that the cause of order probably bears some remote analogy to human intelligence, allows plain philosophical assent to it, and denies it can be extended or yield any practical inference.

Presses the organic resemblance — circulation, repair, sympathy of parts — to infer that the world is an animal and the Deity its soul, judging the ancient theory juster than the modern workmanship analogy.
